title: Year three opens: the story after Acts
hook: the Church keeps its history honestly: holiness and failure side by side

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of year two: the road to Emmaus, every page pointing to Christ. Your line was the book is a person. Which book did you choose to keep reading? Day six hundred ninety-seven.

The Acts of the Apostles ends in a rented room in Rome. Paul is under guard, waiting for his case to be heard. Acts says he stayed there two whole years, welcomed everyone who came to him, and preached without anyone stopping him. And then the book simply stops. No verdict. No trial. Not a word about how Paul dies, or Peter either. The story the Bible tells about the Church breaks off with a door open and visitors still coming in. Year three walks through that door: the long story of the Church after Acts.
screen: `A RENTED ROOM IN ROME.` → `NO VERDICT, NO TRIAL.` → `THE BOOK SIMPLY STOPS.`

segments.voice: Here are the last words of Acts, in the Douay-Rheims: "Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition." After that, the record passes to other hands: letters from bishops, accounts of martyrs, sermons, councils, chronicles. Church history is the name for that long record, and this year we walk through it in order. First, a warning built into the Gospels themselves. They don't hide the failures of the first disciples. Peter, the rock, denies Jesus by a charcoal fire. The others scatter. Paul admits he once hunted Christians down. If the first leaders are shown with their faults, the story after them was never going to be clean. Second, a parable from Matthew: the wheat and the cockle. A man sows good seed, an enemy sows weeds in the night, and the servants want to rip them out. The master says, in the Douay, "Suffer both to grow until the harvest." Saint Augustine read that field as a picture of the Church in this age: good and bad growing in the same soil, sorted only at the end. Third, what that means for the year ahead. You'll meet martyrs who forgave the crowds that killed them, monks who fed the hungry, and a woman who told a pope to go home to Rome. You'll also meet crusades, inquisitions, corrupt bishops, and the wounds of abuse. Catholic teaching calls the Church holy because of Christ, and says plainly that it is always in need of being purified, because its members sin. A pope in our own times publicly asked forgiveness for wrongs done by Christians. Fourth, why tell it this way. A history with only saints would be a statue, not a family. Honest history lets the holiness show against the real background, and it leaves room for ordinary people, who are a bit of both.
screen: `THE GOSPELS DON'T HIDE FAILURE.` · `THE WHEAT AND THE COCKLE.` · `MARTYRS AND CRUSADES, BOTH AHEAD.` · `A FAMILY, NOT A STATUE.` · then, large: `SUFFER BOTH TO GROW UNTIL THE HARVEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of your own family's history of faith. Settle, and breathe. Go back as far as you can: a parent, a grandparent, someone further back whose name you only half remember. Who prayed? Who stopped? Who kept a rosary in a drawer, or argued with a priest, or walked away and came back? Let the good and the hard sit side by side, the way they really were. If your family has no faith story, remember whoever first showed you what kindness looks like. If you pray, you can name each of them before God. The bell holds the time.
Church history. The long record of the Church after Acts, told with its holiness and its failures side by side. Today's word.
Your line: saints and sinners, both. Today, when you hear a story about the Church, good or bad, ask what the other half of it might be. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics learn the Church's history through the saints of the calendar, parish and family stories, and the Church's own teaching, which calls the Church holy while saying its members always need purifying and forgiveness.

fork.setup: you're a servant in the field. weeds have come up among the wheat overnight. what do you do?
options: let both grow until the harvest.
burn the whole field and start again.
fork.reveal: the servants want to pull them up, but the master says wait: pulling the weeds would uproot the wheat too. the sorting comes at the harvest.

notes: Acts 28:31 and Matthew 13:30 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording: confirm exact text.
Augustine's reading of the wheat and tares as the mixed Church: confirm best reference (anti-Donatist writings; also City of God 20.9).
'is always in need of being purified' paraphrases Lumen Gentium 8 (sancta simul et semper purificanda): confirm phrasing is acceptable as a paraphrase.

'Popes in our own times have publicly asked forgiveness for wrongs done by Christians' refers to John Paul II's Day of Pardon (Lent 2000) and later apologies; no date given in script on purpose. Confirm wording.
'a young woman who told a pope to go home to Rome' anticipates Catherine of Siena later in year three; confirm it fits the year-three outline.
Mention of abuse is brief and non-dramatic; Keeper to confirm tone.
